clue.text: Unusually, need import for exchange

indicators.note: something done unusually is done in a strange way, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: the two words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: A trader remarks that, for once, a deal requires bringing goods in from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Import' and 'exchange' both sound like trade, but 'exchange' is the definition, in the sense of cashing something in.
explanation.definitionFit: Redemption is the act of trading in a voucher or coupon for goods or cash, a kind of swap.

clue.text: Large number in service before time

blocks.note: the Royal Air Force is one of the armed services
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Many people are serving in the forces before their time is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply places the service ahead of the time. 'Large number' is not a number like a thousand but an informal word for a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A raft of things is an informal expression for a great many of them, as in a raft of new measures.

clue.text: Notice old man in study giving little away

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one pair of pieces goes inside another

blocks.note: an ad is a notice advertising something
pa is an informal word for father
a den is a private room for work, a study

explanation.surface: Someone spots their father sitting in the study, keeping his feelings to himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The notice and the old man are joined first, then placed inside the study to give DE-ADPA-N.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan face or manner shows no emotion, so it reveals nothing of what the person thinks.

clue.text: Scotsman, maybe – a villain, he's horribly devious

indicators.note: something done horribly is done badly and messily, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: Mac is a familiar way of addressing a Scotsman, from the common surname prefix
taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A Scottish rogue is described as dreadfully sly and untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' tells you the Scotsman is only an example: MAC is a stock way of addressing one.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Niccolò Machiavelli, whose political advice became shorthand for cunning, scheming and unscrupulous behaviour.

clue.text: Cut short drive with jazz fan in centre of Cheltenham

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the innermost letters are kept
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: to run a vehicle or business is to drive it
cat is old slang for a jazz enthusiast
the two central letters of the ten-letter town name

explanation.surface: A jazz lover's trip ends early in the middle of Cheltenham, a spa town in Gloucestershire.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheltenham has ten letters, so its centre is the fifth and sixth, T and E, which wrap around the drive and the jazz fan.
explanation.definitionFit: To truncate is to shorten something by removing its end, exactly what cutting it short means.

clue.text: Stop ticket-holder, showing nerve?

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective naming a kind of nerve, hence the question mark

indicators.note: a holder contains something, so the answer sits inside the preceding words

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A conductor halts a passenger who is being cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nerve' here is anatomical, not cheek: the optic nerve carries signals from the eye, and the question mark flags that the answer only qualifies the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The optic nerve is the one linking eye and brain, so the word identifies a particular nerve by example.

clue.text: Very long shot, backing front-runner in Epsom

indicators.note: the front-runner of a word is whatever leads it, its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the racecourse town
pic is short for picture, a photographic shot

explanation.surface: A punter backs a rank outsider to lead at Epsom, the Surrey racecourse that hosts the Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: In the racing picture 'long shot' and 'backing' are betting terms; cryptically the photo comes behind, backing up, the letter from Epsom.
explanation.definitionFit: Something epic is huge in scale, and the word is commonly used of a journey or film that goes on extremely long.

clue.text: Dangerous leaving son close to heater in room

indicators.note: when something is leaving it goes away, so a letter departs from the word
the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used
here 'in' only marks the room as the result, the pieces simply follow one another

blocks.note: parlous means precarious or perilous
S is the abbreviation for son
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Warning that it is risky for a boy to stand near the fire in the sitting room.
explanation.walkthrough: Parlous is an old variant of perilous; drop its S and add the R that ends the heater.
explanation.definitionFit: A parlour is an old-fashioned sitting room in a house, kept for receiving guests.

clue.text: Green plan: recycle!

blocks.note: a chart can be a plan or map
to recycle is to use again

explanation.surface: An environmental slogan urging people to recycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' sits naturally with recycling as an eco word, but it is the definition, a colour; 'recycle!' is not an anagram signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartreuse is a yellowish-green colour named after the liqueur made by Carthusian monks.

clue.text: Foreign money smuggled into football club

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: to run goods is to smuggle them, past tense ran
FC is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Overseas cash is illicitly funnelled into a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: Gun-running and rum-running give the sense of 'run' as smuggle.
explanation.definitionFit: The franc was the currency of France and Belgium and is still used in Switzerland, so it is overseas money to a Briton.

clue.text: Complaint, having grasped the nettle?

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom for tackling a difficult problem boldly
setter's reading: a medical condition you get from literally holding a stinging plant

explanation.surface: Someone who has finally dealt with a tough issue now has a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grasped the nettle' reads as the idiom for facing a problem, but taken literally it leaves a rash, and 'complaint' means an ailment, not a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Urticaria is the medical name for nettle rash or hives, from Latin urtica, the stinging plant.

clue.text: Ancient doer of wrong in alliance

indicators.note: something put wrong is out of its proper order, so these letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the three words give all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: An old wrongdoer turns out to be part of a league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doer of wrong' reads as a criminal, but 'wrong' is the anagram signal and 'of' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A confederation is a union of states or groups joined for common purposes, which is a league or alliance.

clue.text: Albert, perhaps, arranged prison concert

indicators.note: to arrange something is to set it in a new order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the two words supply all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: Someone called Albert has organised a gig inside a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' fits the concert as a musical arrangement, but it signals the letters are reordered. 'perhaps' marks Albert as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Albert, husband of Queen Victoria, was formally given the title of royal consort, the reigning queen's husband.

clue.text: Freedom to pass that's okay, following approach

blocks.note: righto is a British exclamation of agreement
f is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a way of doing something is an approach to it

explanation.surface: Permission to go through is given with an approving word as someone draws near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' looks like a positional link, but it supplies a single letter, as in 'pp 10f'. The chunks cut across the word breaks of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A right of way is a legal entitlement to go across land or to proceed ahead of other traffic.

clue.text: Creatively design home without tax – Angela's fourth?

indicators.note: fourth names a position, so only the letter in that place of the name is taken

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
no means none or lacking, so it can stand for without
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax
the fourth letter of the name

explanation.surface: An architect, Angela, devises her fourth tax-free house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like a container or deletion signal but here it is simply the word NO, as in 'no money' meaning without money.
explanation.definitionFit: To innovate is to introduce new methods or ideas, which is coming up with something original.

clue.text: Order always withdrawn after the last month

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so the word runs backwards
after places one piece to follow another in sequence

blocks.note: December is the final month of the year, abbreviated
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: An instruction that has stood for ever is cancelled at the end of December.
explanation.walkthrough: E'er is a poetic form of ever, meaning always.
explanation.definitionFit: A decree is an official order issued by a ruler or court that has the force of law.

clue.text: Plucky type of performer seen in olden times?

definitions.text: Plucky type of performer seen in olden times?

blocks.note: surface reading: a brave, spirited sort of person
setter's reading: a medieval entertainer who plucked the strings of a lute or harp

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucky' means courageous on the surface, but here it means one who plucks strings.
explanation.definitionFit: In medieval times a wandering musician sang and played stringed instruments for nobles at court.

clue.text: Exert pressure on crowd

blocks.note: first meaning: to push someone into acting quickly
second meaning: to jostle or shove people

explanation.walkthrough: 'crowd' reads as a noun, a mass of people, but it is a verb meaning to press on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both pushing someone into a decision and roughly shoving people about in a throng.

clue.text: Seen in Trieste, a merchant vessel

indicators.note: something seen in a phrase is visible within it, so the answer lies inside these words

blocks.note: runs from the end of the port name through the start of the third word

explanation.surface: A cargo ship is spotted in the Italian port of Trieste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'merchant vessel' looks like a single definition, but the start of 'merchant' supplies the last letters, leaving 'vessel' alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A steamer is a ship driven by steam power, one kind of seagoing boat.

clue.text: Slipped over having grabbed book offering puzzles

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the word is read in the opposite direction
grabbing something means holding it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: slid is the past tense of slide, to slip
Emma is a novel by Jane Austen

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles while clutching a book of brainteasers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'book' does not mean B here; it is a specific title, Jane Austen's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dilemmas are perplexing problems involving a hard choice, so they can be called puzzles.

clue.text: Slander hospital, receiving stick for spa treatment?

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece is put inside the others

blocks.note: to sling mud is to slander, so mud is defamation
H is the abbreviation for hospital
a bat is a stick used in sport, as in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: A patient is abused and beaten with a stick when going to a health resort.
explanation.walkthrough: The slander and hospital are joined, then the stick goes between them. The question mark nods at a mud bath being a messy treat.
explanation.definitionFit: Spas offer baths in warm mineral mud, believed to soothe the skin and joints, as a therapy.

clue.text: Brief encounter: snog and then it's done!

definitions.text: Brief encounter: snog and then it's done!

blocks.note: surface reading: the title of the classic 1945 British film about a chaste romance
setter's reading: a fleeting sexual fling that lasts only the one evening

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief Encounter' calls to mind the David Lean film of a restrained wartime affair; read plainly it is a short liaison. 'Snog' is British slang for a passionate kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a casual romantic or sexual encounter between people who do not meet again after one evening.

clue.text: Leader abandoning simple expedition

indicators.note: when the leader abandons a word its opening letter is lost

blocks.note: chaste can mean plain and simple in style

explanation.surface: A team leader pulls out of a modest trek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expedition' reads as a journey, but its older sense is speed or promptness, as in 'with all expedition'.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition can mean speed or promptness in doing something, which is what hurry means.

clue.text: Send bride-to-be amazing trousers

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so the answer is tucked inside these words

blocks.note: spans the end of the compound and the start of the adjective

explanation.surface: An instruction to dispatch some stunning trousers to a fiancée.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' looks like a noun, the garment, but it is the verb 'trouser', British slang for to pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: To beam a signal or message is to transmit it, for example by radio or satellite.

clue.text: Possibly a winsome Romeo?

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several versions, so the letters may be set in another order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A charming lover, perhaps one who pursues many women.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo does double duty: a letter for the wordplay, and as a whole clue the sort of charming seducer the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A romeo is a man with many love affairs, and one who is appealing could well be a serial seducer.

clue.text: It may get endless representation

indicators.note: without an end, so each word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something may receive an unending depiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' applies to all three preceding words, not just one, so each is clipped by a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture or likeness, a visual depiction of someone or something.

clue.text: Story's thread

blocks.note: first meaning: a long rambling tale
second meaning: spun fibre for knitting or weaving

explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive, the thread of a story, but it is 'is', joining two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a long, often tall tale and spun wool or fibre used in knitting.

clue.text: Footballer, big name, he'll burst having eliminated Spain

indicators.note: something that bursts is blown apart, so the letters scatter into a new order
to eliminate something is to remove it, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A star player will be a sensation once his team knocks Spain out.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one of the two Es in the fodder goes. Jude Bellingham is an England midfielder who played for Real Madrid, a nice nod to Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Jude Bellingham is a celebrated English international footballer, so he is an example of the profession.
